title: De Ecclesiasticis Dogmatibus (Incertus)
author: Isidorus Hispalensis
source: Translated by Claude from tmp1437.tmp1437.opp-lat1, as held by Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.
availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

passages.original: Creditur a nobis sine confusione eonjuncta sancta Trinitas, sine separatione distincta. Naius est ergo Dei Filius ex homine, et non per hominem, id est, non ex viri coitu, sicut Ebion dicit ; sed carnem ex Virginis corpore trahens, et non de cœlo secum alTerens, sicut Marcion, Origenes et Eutyches affirmant. Neque in phantasia, id est, absque carne, sicut Valeniinus asserit, id est, neque putative imaginatum, sed corpus veram. Non tantum carnem ex carne, sicut Marcianus, sed verus Deus ex divinitate et verus bomo ex carne, unus Filius ;
passages.english: We believe the holy Trinity to be joined without confusion and distinct without separation. The Son of God, then, was born of a human being, and not through a man, that is, not from intercourse with a man, as Ebion says; but taking flesh from the body of the Virgin, and not bringing [it] with him from heaven, as Marcion, Origen and Eutyches affirm. Nor [was he born] in appearance, that is, without flesh, as Valentinus asserts, that is, not imagined in supposition, but [with] a true body. Not only flesh from flesh, as Marcianus [holds], but true God from the divinity and true man from the flesh, one Son;
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected silently (eonjuncta, Naius, alTerens, Valeniinus, veram, bomo). 'Marcianus' is uncertain; perhaps a corruption of a heresiarch's name (e.g. Marcion or Marcellus).

passages.original: Nihil creatum aut serviens In Trinitate credamus, ut vult Dionysius, fons Arii ; nihil inæquale, ut vult Eunomius, ut Arius; nihil inæquale gratiæ,ut vult Aetius; nibil auterius posteriusve, aut minus, ut Arius; nihil extraneum, aut ofliciale alteri, ut Macedonius; nihil persuasione aut subreptione insertum, ut Manichæus ; nihil corporeum, ut Melito et Tertullianus ; nihil corporaliter effigiatum, ut Anthropomorphus, et Vadianus ; nihil sibi invisibile a creaturis, ut Origenes; nihil creaturis visibile, ut Fortunatus; nihil moribus vel voluntate diversum, ut Alarcion; nihil ex Trinitatis essentia ad creaturarum naturam deduetum, ut Plato et Tertultianus ; nihil efficio singulave, nec alteri commuuicabile, ut Origenes ; nitri confusum, ut Sabellius ; sed totum perfectum, quia totum ex imo, et unum ex toto ; non tamen solitarium, ut præsumunt Praxeas et Salvanus, Pentapolitana damnabilis illa doctrina.
passages.english: Let us believe nothing in the Trinity to be created or subservient, as Dionysius, the source of Arius, would have it; nothing unequal, as Eunomius would have it, [and] as Arius; nothing unequal in grace, as Aetius would have it; nothing earlier or later, or lesser, as Arius; nothing foreign, or performing service for another, as Macedonius; nothing inserted by persuasion or by stealth, as Manichaeus; nothing bodily, as Melito and Tertullian; nothing given bodily shape, as the Anthropomorphite and Audianus; nothing invisible to itself [but visible] to creatures, as Origen; nothing visible to creatures, as Fortunatus; nothing differing in character or will, as Marcion; nothing derived from the essence of the Trinity into the nature of creatures, as Plato and Tertullian; nothing peculiar to one or single, and not communicable to another, as Origen; nothing confused, as Sabellius; but [let us believe] the whole perfect, because the whole is from one, and one from the whole; yet not solitary, as Praxeas and Sabellius presume, that damnable Pentapolitan doctrine.
passages.notes: 'nihil sibi invisibile a creaturis' is obscure; perhaps 'nothing invisible to itself' (i.e. Father not seen by Son); rendering tentative. 'efficio' read as 'proprium' (peculiar), a guess. 'Vadianus' read as Audianus; 'Salvanus' taken as a corruption of Sabellius (Pentapolitan heresy). Other scanning errors corrected (ofliciale, nitri, imo = uno, auterius = prius).

passages.original: Quod autem dicimus in Symbolo, in adventu Domini vivos ac rnortuos judicandos, non solum justos et peccatores signilicari, sicut Diodorus putat, sed et vivos eos qui in carne inveniendi sunt, credimus, qui adhuc morituri creduntur, vel immutandi sunt, ut alii volunt, ut suscitati continuo, vel reformati, cum ante mortuis judicentur.
passages.english: As for what we say in the Creed, that at the coming of the Lord the living and the dead are to be judged, we believe that this signifies not only the just and sinners, as Diodorus thinks, but also as "the living" those who will be found in the flesh, who are believed still to be going to die, or are to be changed, as others hold, so that, raised at once or re-formed, they may be judged together with those who died before.
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected: 'rnortuos' for 'mortuos', 'signilicari' for 'significari'. The final clause 'cum ante mortuis' is read as 'together with those who died before'. The text may be corrupt here.

passages.original: Animas hominum non esse ab initio inter caeteras intellectuales naturas, nec insimul creatas, sicut Origenes fingit; neque cum corporibus per coitum seminantur, sicut Luciferiani, Cyrillus et aliqui Latinorum praesumptores affirmant, quasi naturae consequentiam servantes. Sed dicimus creationem animae solum Creatorem omnium nosse, et corpus tantum per conjugii copulam seminari, Dei vero judicio coagulari in vulva, et compingi, atque forrnari, ac formato jam corpore animam creari, et infundi, ut vivat in utero homo ex anima constans et corpore, et egrediatur vivus ex utero plenus humana substantia.
passages.english: [We hold] that the souls of human beings did not exist from the beginning among the other intellectual natures, nor were they created all together, as Origen imagines. Nor are they sown together with bodies through intercourse, as the Luciferians, Cyril and certain presumptuous Latin writers affirm, as though preserving the logical sequence of nature. Rather, we say that the Creator of all alone knows the creation of the soul. Only the body is sown through the union of marriage, but by the judgement of God it is coagulated in the womb, and put together, and formed. Once the body has been formed, the soul is created and infused, so that the human being may live in the womb, consisting of soul and body, and may come forth alive from the womb, complete in human substance.
passages.notes: 'forrnari' read as 'formari'. 'Cyrillus' as an advocate of traducianism is an odd attribution; the name may be corrupt.

passages.original: Solum hominem credimus habere animam substantivam, quae exula corpore vivit, et sensus suos atque ingenia vivaciter tenet. Non cum corpore moritur, sicut Aratus asserit, neque post modicum intervallum, sicut Zenon dicit, quia substantialiter vivit.
passages.english: We believe that only the human being has a substantial soul, which lives when separated from the body and keeps its senses and faculties in vigour. It does not die with the body, as Aratus asserts, nor after a short interval, as Zeno says, because it lives substantially.
passages.notes: 'exula corpore' read as 'exuta corpore' (stripped of the body). 'Aratus' is uncertain; it may stand for another name, perhaps Aristotle or Aristoxenus.

passages.original: Animalium vero animae non sunt substantivae, sed cum carne ipsa carnis vivacitate nascuntur, et cum earuis morte finiuntur, et moriuntur; et ideo nec ratione reguntur, sicut Plato et Alexander putant, sed ad omnia naturae incitamenta ducuntur.
passages.english: The souls of animals, however, are not substantial. They are born with the flesh itself, by the vitality of the flesh, and with the death of the flesh they come to an end and die. Therefore they are not governed by reason, as Plato and Alexander think, but are led by all the promptings of nature.
passages.notes: 'earuis' read as 'carnis'. 'Alexander' is not certainly identified; possibly Alexander of Aphrodisias.

passages.original: Neque enim credendum est eos fuisse baptizatos, qui non in nomine Patris, et Filii, et Spiritus sancti, juxta regulam a Domino positam, tincti sunt, ut Paulini Procliani, Borboritæ, Siphori, qui nunc vocantur Bonostani, Photiniani, Montani, et Manichæi, variaque impietatis germina, vel caeterae istorum originis, sive ordinis pestes, quae duo principia sibi ignota introducunt, ut Cerdon et Marcion; vel contraria, ut Manichæus; vel tria, et barbara, ut Sethianus, et Theodosius; vel multa, ut Valentinus; vel Christum hominem fuisse absque Deo, ut Cerinthus, Hebion, Artemon, et Photinus. Ex istis, inquam, si qui ad nos venerint, non requirendum ab eis utrum baptizati sint, an non;
passages.english: For it must not be believed that those were baptized who were not dipped in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, according to the rule laid down by the Lord, such as the Paulianists, Proclianists, Borborites, Siphori (who are now called Bonosians), Photinians, Montanists and Manichaeans, and the various shoots of impiety, or the other plagues of their origin or order, which introduce two principles unknown to each other, as Cerdo and Marcion; or opposed [principles], as Manichaeus; or three, and barbarous ones, as Sethianus and Theodosius; or many, as Valentinus; or [who hold] that Christ was a man without God, as Cerinthus, Ebion, Artemon and Photinus. Of these, I say, if any come to us, it is not to be asked of them whether they have been baptized or not;
passages.notes: 'Siphori' and 'Bonostani' (Bonosians?) uncertain; 'Theodosius' among those positing three principles is unidentified. 'sibi ignota' perhaps 'unknown to one another'.

passages.original: In divinis promissionibus nibil terrenum vel transitorium exspectemus , sicut Meletiani sperant; non nuptiarum copulam, sicut Cerinthius et Marcion delirant; non quod ad cibum vel ad potum pertinet, sicut Papiae, auctore Irenæo, et Tertullianus et Lactantius acquiescunt. Neque per mille annos post resurrectionem regnum Christi in terra iuturum, et sanctos cum illo in deliciis regnaturos speremus, sicut Nepos docuit, primam justorum resurrectionem et secundam impiorum qui confinxit;
passages.english: In the divine promises let us expect nothing earthly or transitory, as the Meletians hope; not the union of marriage, as Cerinthus and Marcion rave; not what pertains to food or drink, as Papias, on the authority of Irenaeus, and Tertullian and Lactantius accept. Nor let us hope that for a thousand years after the resurrection there will be a kingdom of Christ on earth, and that the saints will reign with him in delights, as Nepos taught, who invented a first resurrection of the just and a second of the wicked;
passages.notes: 'Papiae' read as Papias. 'Meletiani' perhaps a corruption (e.g. Melitiani/Millenarians); uncertain.
